findings.source_passage: The sport was a new one to him. Though familiar with the technicalities from a course of novel reading, he had never before attempted to 'follow' anyone, and it appeared to him at once that, in actual practice, the proceeding was fraught with difficulties.
findings.why_it_matters: Christie's ironic contrast between novel-reading theory and 'actual practice' is a voice-establishing comic digression that frames Tommy as an amateur hero; the draft reduces it to a single parenthetical clause ('new to the sport he knew only from novels'), losing the sustained ironic register.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore at least two sentences of Tommy's internal reasoning about the gap between fictional and real surveillance, including the 'fraught with difficulties' framing and the taxi-sovereign observation.

findings.source_passage: In books, you simply leapt into another, promised the driver a sovereign--or its modern equivalent--and there you were. In actual fact, Tommy foresaw that it was extremely likely there would be no second taxi.
findings.why_it_matters: This passage is the comic heart of the novel-reader-vs-reality motif that Christie deploys throughout; the parenthetical 'or its modern equivalent' is a characteristically Christiean ironic aside and the whole passage is interpretively important as Tommy's self-aware amateurism.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the taxi-sovereign passage verbatim or near-verbatim as it is a signature ironic aside that establishes Tommy's character and Christie's playful narrator-voice.

findings.source_passage: What he ought to have done, what any sane man would have done, was to remain patiently where he was and wait for his man to come out again. What he did do was entirely foreign to the sober common sense which was, as a rule, his leading characteristic.
findings.source_locator: Penultimate action paragraph, before Tommy knocks
findings.why_it_matters: Christie's ironic narratorial aside about Tommy's 'sober common sense' is both textually distinctive and characterologically significant; the draft reduces it to 'Tommy's common sense should have kept him where he was. Something in his brain snapped,' losing the ironic double-take and the narratorial voice.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the two-sentence contrast ('What he ought to have done... What he did do...') which is a signature Christie narratorial intrusion; 'sober common sense which was, as a rule, his leading characteristic' should be preserved as it is distinctively ironic and character-defining.

findings.source_passage: he had a full view of the second man and studied him attentively. He was fair, with a weak, unpleasant face, and Tommy put him down as being either a Russian or a Pole.
findings.source_locator: Lyons' café paragraph, character description of Boris
findings.why_it_matters: The phrase 'put him down as being either a Russian or a Pole' carries Christie's period character-typing voice and is part of how she establishes the novel's atmosphere of foreign menace; the draft omits this inference.
findings.suggested_fix: Add the 'Russian or a Pole' inference to preserve Christie's period voice in the character sketch of Boris.

summary: The draft preserves all plot beats and the key signature dialogue (Flossie, Mr. Brown soliloquy, millionaire exchange) but flattens Christie's sustained ironic-amateur-hero voice in the pursuit prologue and the 'sober common sense' aside, two medium-severity voice losses that do not individually trigger regeneration.
